title: Chainalysis Finds $443B MENA Crypto Economy as UAE Growth Outpaces Region
summary: The United Arab Emirates was reported to have grown 32% to about $104.8 billion, while Türkiye remained larger at around $144.5 billion. The
content:
TL;DR: The United Arab Emirates was reported to have grown 32% to about $104.8 billion, while Türkiye remained larger at around $144.5 billion. The reporting period ends in June 2026, so its totals should not be presented as October market activity.

Chainalysis reported roughly $443.3 billion in cryptocurrency value received across the Middle East and North Africa during its July 2025–June 2026 study period, a decline of 1.4%. The study noted sharply different trajectories between individual countries.

The announcement and the numbers

The most concrete starting point is the dated disclosure from Chainalysis. It offers a specific basis for assessing Chainalysis’s 2026 Middle East and North Africa crypto adoption analysis without turning the story into unsupported price speculation.

The United Arab Emirates was reported to have grown 32% to about $104.8 billion, while Türkiye remained larger at around $144.5 billion. Chainalysis also pointed to a fivefold rise in Turkish domestic peer-to-peer stablecoin volume and interruptions to Iranian activity during internet blackouts.

The development arrives as digital-asset markets remain sensitive to funding conditions, infrastructure reliability and the gap between promotional claims and operational results. It warrants attention on its own facts, without assuming a particular cryptocurrency must rise or fall in response.

Why the development matters

The question for market participants is what Chainalysis’s 2026 Middle East and North Africa crypto adoption analysis establishes today and what remains uncertain. An immediate reaction is not the same as evidence of a durable economic outcome.

One regional average hides the different reasons people use cryptocurrency. Licensing can restructure the business landscape; inflation or currency access can influence stablecoin demand; network shutdowns can temporarily suppress the transactions analysts can observe.

Regional crypto usage reflects differences in banking access, remittances, regulation, inflation and technology. A rise in transaction value does not necessarily mean a proportional rise in individuals using digital assets to buy everyday goods.

Investors also need to separate changes in infrastructure from changes in token demand. Revenue may accrue to a company, a protocol treasury or a service provider without necessarily creating a one-for-one benefit for holders of a related token. Market impact depends on adoption, competition and the design of whatever fees or incentives are involved.

Risks the headline does not resolve

None of this removes the need for independent assessment. The published evidence identifies a development, while its risk and long-term economics are still open to examination.

On-chain measures capture transfers visible to analytical models, not every retail purchase or unique individual. Large institutional transactions, exchange transfers, currency hedging and remittances can all affect headline values.

The reporting period ends in June 2026, so its totals should not be presented as October market activity. Estimates are also sensitive to attribution methods and the range of services the analyst can identify on-chain.

When evaluating an adoption report, readers should examine the measurement period, what types of transfers are counted and how the analyst handles unidentified entities. Comparisons are most useful when the method is broadly consistent across countries.

The milestones to watch

The immediate checklist is relatively straightforward: look for verifiable implementation details and avoid interpreting a stated target as an outcome that has already occurred.

Future research should help distinguish durable merchant and remittance use from exchange churn, examine how new regulations affect licensed activity and track the resilience of payment channels during network disruptions.

A durable signal would be consistent follow-through: actual usage, transparent reporting and a credible explanation of risk. Short-term token-price moves can be driven by macroeconomic conditions or leverage and may say little about whether the product or initiative succeeds over months and years.

From a market perspective, the first task is to separate the scale of the announcement from the scale of economic activity that has actually occurred. A company may report a large addressable market, an institutional name or a future capability, but those are not equivalent to settled transactions or recurring fee income. This is why the primary disclosure is a better starting point than a trading narrative attached to it.

Primary source: Chainalysis’s primary announcement. This reporting reflects information available on October 31, 2026; targets, estimates and statements about future plans are attributed to their issuers.

This article was written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Michael Saylor Sees Stronger Crypto Security After Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack
summary: Michael Saylor expects the crypto industry to strengthen security after Binance’s $6.3 billion hack. The Strategy executive chairman also backed the exchange’s commitment to use its own balance sheet to make customers whole. Saylor Sees Lessons From Binance Security Failures Strategy Inc. (Nasdaq: M...
content:
Michael Saylor expects the crypto industry to strengthen security after Binance’s $6.3 billion hack. The Strategy executive chairman also backed the exchange’s commitment to use its own balance sheet to make customers whole.

Key Takeaways

  • Binance said $5 billion was already held in the affected cryptocurrencies.
  • About $3 billion in stolen assets had been frozen, the exchange reported.
  • Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the attacker bypassed normal approval controls.

Saylor Sees Lessons From Binance Security Failures

Strategy Inc. (Nasdaq: MSTR) Executive Chairman Michael Saylor said on Oct. 30 that the crypto industry would improve its defenses following Binance’s estimated $6.3 billion hack. In his assessment of Binance’s response, shared on X, he stated:

“Binance has committed its own balance sheet to making customers whole. I expect it to deliver. Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security, and emerge stronger and more resilient.”

The exchange’s official security update, also dated Oct. 30, placed the hot-wallet compromise at approximately 8:05 p.m. UTC on Oct. 29. Binance pledged coverage through its corporate treasury and Secure Asset Fund for Users, or SAFU, an emergency fund to protect user assets. The company said investigators had uncovered breach points beyond the initially suspected compromised laptop and found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked.

Saylor’s remarks followed Strategy’s record third-quarter results, announced Oct. 29, which included $20.91 billion in operating income and $44.75 in diluted earnings per share. The company held 848,517 bitcoin as of Oct. 25, up 26% year to date. Saylor said a new bitcoin bull market was beginning, citing growing institutional demand and banks’ adoption of bitcoin.

Company Funds Back Asset Replacement

More than $6.34 billion in company funds had been reserved for the incident, according to Binance. Of that amount, $5 billion was already held in the affected cryptocurrencies, while purchases through market and over-the-counter channels were intended to fill remaining shortfalls. Limited liquidity in some tokens and settlement times could slow those purchases, the company said.

Separately, Binance reported approximately $3 billion in frozen stolen assets, distinct from its replacement funds, as it pursued recovery with law enforcement and industry partners. Its withdrawal recovery plan targeted a phased restart within approximately 34 hours of the Oct. 30 update, subject to completed security checks. Updated proof-of-reserves results were planned by Nov. 3.

Security Review Examines Devices and Transfer Approvals

Co-CEO Richard Teng described an expanded security investigation in a video shared on Oct. 30, saying the attacker bypassed normal approval controls and used a self-destruct mechanism to erase tools and traces. The companywide review covered endpoints, such as employee computers connected to its network, along with cloud infrastructure and key management. It also examined transaction-signing systems that authorize cryptocurrency transfers.

Most customer assets were held in cold wallets, with transfers into hot wallets supporting withdrawals, Teng said. Offline private-key storage keeps keys disconnected from the internet, while exchange-held cold wallets remain under the provider’s custody. Binance also planned a technical postmortem, a detailed review of how the attack occurred and the safeguards being implemented.

title: Further Asset Management Taps Chainlink ACE for Abu Dhabi Compliance Platform
summary: The company described jurisdiction-specific rules that can be encoded into workflows so institutions can assess requirements before a tokenized asset
content:
TL;DR: The company described jurisdiction-specific rules that can be encoded into workflows so institutions can assess requirements before a tokenized asset moves. A machine-readable rule is only as sound as its legal interpretation, reference data and update process.

Further Asset Management said on October 27 that its Anubis compliance platform would incorporate Chainlink’s Automated Compliance Engine, with an initial focus on institutional tokenized-asset operations inside Abu Dhabi Global Market.

The announcement and the numbers

The most concrete starting point is the dated disclosure from Further Asset Management. It offers a specific basis for assessing Further Asset Management’s machine-readable tokenized-asset compliance plan without turning the story into unsupported price speculation.

The company described jurisdiction-specific rules that can be encoded into workflows so institutions can assess requirements before a tokenized asset moves. The initial deployment is intended to align with relevant Financial Services Regulatory Authority expectations in ADGM.

Announcements in crypto often arrive before the data needed to price their longer-term significance. A sensible reading separates what has already been delivered from what still needs commercial adoption, technical validation or regulatory clearance.

Why the development matters

The question for market participants is what Further Asset Management’s machine-readable tokenized-asset compliance plan establishes today and what remains uncertain. An immediate reaction is not the same as evidence of a durable economic outcome.

Automating restrictions can reduce operational friction if regulated firms share a consistent approach. It also highlights why the real-world asset market needs more than low-cost blockchain transactions: investors need evidence that rights and eligibility remain enforceable.

A pilot, framework or technical partnership should not be conflated with a live secondary market. Investors need to know whether assets have actually been issued, whether redemption is possible and where responsibility sits if records disagree.

A durable signal would be consistent follow-through: actual usage, transparent reporting and a credible explanation of risk. Short-term token-price moves can be driven by macroeconomic conditions or leverage and may say little about whether the product or initiative succeeds over months and years.

Risks the headline does not resolve

None of this removes the need for independent assessment. The published evidence identifies a development, while its risk and long-term economics are still open to examination.

Tokenization can make asset transfers programmable, but it does not make securities law or client restrictions disappear. A policy engine checks what a participant may do, which asset is involved and which legal or geographic conditions apply to the proposed action.

A machine-readable rule is only as sound as its legal interpretation, reference data and update process. Regulatory changes, exceptions and manual review requirements can create edge cases that software cannot settle simply by checking a field.

Representing an asset on a blockchain is the relatively straightforward part of tokenization. Making that representation useful requires legal rights, reliable valuation, restrictions on eligible holders, custody and a clear process for settlement and corporate actions.

The milestones to watch

The immediate checklist is relatively straightforward: look for verifiable implementation details and avoid interpreting a stated target as an outcome that has already occurred.

Observers should look for actual compliant asset workflows, auditability and whether other regulated firms adopt the model. The announced integration is a technical and commercial step, not proof of broad legal approval for every product built using it.

From a market perspective, the first task is to separate the scale of the announcement from the scale of economic activity that has actually occurred. A company may report a large addressable market, an institutional name or a future capability, but those are not equivalent to settled transactions or recurring fee income. This is why the primary disclosure is a better starting point than a trading narrative attached to it.

Investors also need to separate changes in infrastructure from changes in token demand. Revenue may accrue to a company, a protocol treasury or a service provider without necessarily creating a one-for-one benefit for holders of a related token. Market impact depends on adoption, competition and the design of whatever fees or incentives are involved.

title: Trump Speaks on $6.3B Binance Hack as FBI Confirms North Korea
summary: President Donald Trump said U.S. officials were looking into Binance’s $6.3 billion hack and acknowledged the exchange’s recovery assurances. The FBI subsequently attributed the theft to North Korea and warned of further laundering. Trump Examines North Korea Link and Binance Assurances President Do...
content:
President Donald Trump said U.S. officials were looking into Binance’s $6.3 billion hack and acknowledged the exchange’s recovery assurances. The FBI subsequently attributed the theft to North Korea and warned of further laundering.

Key Takeaways

  • Trump addressed the hack before the FBI attributed it to North Korea.
  • North Korean actors converted stolen assets into ether, the bureau said.
  • Binance reported 90% replenishment and targeted a Sunday restart.

Trump Examines North Korea Link and Binance Assurances

President Donald Trump said on Oct. 30 that U.S. officials were looking into the Binance hack and possible North Korean involvement. He spoke during an Oval Office meeting with Stephen Hubbard, an American recently released from a Russian prison.

When asked about North Korean responsibility regarding the hack of Binance, Trump stated:

“We’re looking at that.”

Addressing prospects for recovering the money, Trump cited Binance’s assurances: “Well, they say they’re gonna get it back, and they’re guaranteeing it or something. They are.”

Comparing digital transactions with signing a check, he added: “I’ve always felt it was a little bit dangerous. But no, they say they have it pretty much under control. We’ll see.”

FBI Attributes Binance Attack to North Korea

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) attributed the theft to North Korea on Oct. 31, stating:

“The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026.”

The FBI, the U.S. Secret Service, and the Internal Revenue Service’s Criminal Investigation division observed the attackers converting stolen assets primarily into ether. The bureau expected further conversions through decentralized finance platforms and instant swap services, which exchange one cryptocurrency for another. It identified the North Korean cyber activity as Tradertraitor.

The FBI urged cryptocurrency exchanges, blockchain infrastructure operators, analytics firms, and other digital asset service providers to block transactions involving or originating from addresses used by the attackers. The alert listed addresses associated with laundering the stolen assets and called for private-sector assistance in disrupting those transfers.

Chainalysis and TRM Labs had also attributed the attack to Tradertraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group targeting cryptocurrency platforms and investors. Chainalysis’s North Korea findings included stolen Binance assets mixing with proceeds from September’s Bitget theft, previously attributed to North Korean actors. Separately, TRM Labs expressed high confidence in its assessment, citing onchain and offchain intelligence.

Investigators traced thousands of transfers through public blockchain transaction records, including repeated returns to previously used wallets. Chainalysis said the pattern suggested automated laundering, with software repeatedly moving funds to obscure their origins.

Replacement Purchases Narrow Binance’s Shortfall

Binance’s recovery plan reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds, excluding approximately $3 billion in frozen assets. Matching token holdings initially covered about 80% of losses.

An Oct. 31 update put replenishment at 90% with 10 cryptocurrencies, including BTC, ETH, and XRP, fully backed. Replenishment drew on company funds, its emergency Secure Asset Fund for Users, and futures insurance reserves. Binance was sourcing less liquid tokens to cover the remaining shortfall and pledged to absorb all losses. These purchases replaced affected assets separately from recovering stolen funds.

Withdrawals remained targeted for Sunday, Nov. 1. Binance published a reserve snapshot taken at midnight Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the international time standard, on Oct. 31. The full cryptographic proof was expected by Nov. 3, allowing holders of the 10 listed tokens to verify minimum 1:1 backing.

title: Chainlink Launches CustodySync With Anchorage to Link Custody and DeFi Loans

content:
TL;DR: Chainlink describes a workflow spanning collateral deposit, borrowing, repayment and liquidation. Keeping assets in custody does not automatically remove smart-contract, oracle, liquidation or legal-enforcement risk.

Chainlink announced CustodySync on October 26 with Anchorage Digital as its initial partner. The service aims to synchronize information between qualified custodians and decentralised lending protocols, allowing eligible institutions to borrow against assets while retaining their existing custody arrangements.

The announcement and the numbers

The most concrete starting point is the dated disclosure from Chainlink. It offers a specific basis for assessing Chainlink CustodySync’s institutional lending model without turning the story into unsupported price speculation.

Chainlink describes a workflow spanning collateral deposit, borrowing, repayment and liquidation. Anchorage’s infrastructure and Atlas Collateral Management product are designed to coordinate with lending protocols in an arrangement closer to institutional collateral-agency practices.

The development arrives as digital-asset markets remain sensitive to funding conditions, infrastructure reliability and the gap between promotional claims and operational results. It warrants attention on its own facts, without assuming a particular cryptocurrency must rise or fall in response.

Why the development matters

The question for market participants is what Chainlink CustodySync’s institutional lending model establishes today and what remains uncertain. An immediate reaction is not the same as evidence of a durable economic outcome.

If implemented effectively, this design could expand on-chain credit without asking regulated investors to abandon normal segregation, control and reporting requirements. It is an example of institutional DeFi focusing on legal and operational interfaces rather than offering a higher headline yield.

For developers, execution quality involves more than a quoted price or an advertised feature. Gas costs, settlement success, oracle quality, permissions and incident handling all shape whether an integration is safe and convenient in real markets.

Investors also need to separate changes in infrastructure from changes in token demand. Revenue may accrue to a company, a protocol treasury or a service provider without necessarily creating a one-for-one benefit for holders of a related token. Market impact depends on adoption, competition and the design of whatever fees or incentives are involved.

Risks the headline does not resolve

None of this removes the need for independent assessment. The published evidence identifies a development, while its risk and long-term economics are still open to examination.

Institutions often cannot simply transfer assets out of approved custody to participate in a DeFi protocol. A data and control layer can let different systems attest to the same collateral state while preserving defined restrictions on asset movement.

Keeping assets in custody does not automatically remove smart-contract, oracle, liquidation or legal-enforcement risk. Responsibilities between custodian, lender and collateral agent must be unambiguous when prices move quickly or a loan defaults.

For investors, a protocol upgrade should be distinguished from automatic economic value for a token. Fees, governance, user retention and the distribution of benefits can differ substantially from the headline adoption story.

The milestones to watch

The immediate checklist is relatively straightforward: look for verifiable implementation details and avoid interpreting a stated target as an outcome that has already occurred.

Watch for live loans, participating lending markets, collateral eligibility rules and independently described safeguards. The size of assets in digital custody is an opportunity estimate, not capital already committed to the new product.

A durable signal would be consistent follow-through: actual usage, transparent reporting and a credible explanation of risk. Short-term token-price moves can be driven by macroeconomic conditions or leverage and may say little about whether the product or initiative succeeds over months and years.

From a market perspective, the first task is to separate the scale of the announcement from the scale of economic activity that has actually occurred. A company may report a large addressable market, an institutional name or a future capability, but those are not equivalent to settled transactions or recurring fee income. This is why the primary disclosure is a better starting point than a trading narrative attached to it.

title: The Largest Crypto Hacks in History Ranked by Dollar Value and Bitcoin Stolen
summary: The reported $6.3 billion Binance breach may have rewritten cryptocurrency’s record books in dollar terms, but measuring digital heists in bitcoin paints a strikingly different picture. From Mt Gox’s hundreds of thousands of vanished BTC to Bybit’s $1.5 billion debacle, history’s largest cryptocurre...
content:
The reported $6.3 billion Binance breach may have rewritten cryptocurrency’s record books in dollar terms, but measuring digital heists in bitcoin paints a strikingly different picture. From Mt Gox’s hundreds of thousands of vanished BTC to Bybit’s $1.5 billion debacle, history’s largest cryptocurrency thefts demonstrate how the magnitude of a financial calamity can change dramatically depending on the yardstick used.

Key Takeaways

  • Binance’s reported $6.3 billion breach has eclipsed previous cryptocurrency thefts in dollar terms, but historical bitcoin losses paint a different picture.
  • Mt Gox, Bitfinex and other early incidents involved extraordinary quantities of BTC whose hypothetical present-day valuations dwarf their original losses.
  • Recoveries, customer reimbursements and the proportion of assets affected complicate the question of which cryptocurrency hack was truly the most damaging.

Binance’s $6.3 Billion Disaster Puts Crypto’s Biggest Heists Under the Microscope

Cryptocurrency has produced fortunes, technological breakthroughs, and an extraordinary collection of security disasters. Some attacks exploited sophisticated vulnerabilities in blockchain infrastructure, while others relied on stolen credentials, compromised private keys, or weaknesses in the human beings entrusted with protecting billions of dollars.

The latest reported incident involving Binance has pushed those historical comparisons back into the spotlight. According to the latest findings, approximately $6.3 billion to $6.4 billion in digital assets was removed from Binance wallets on Oct. 29, 2026, potentially making it the largest cryptocurrency theft ever recorded by dollar value. The figures remain provisional, and the estimates attributed to blockchain analytics firms should not be confused with the findings of a completed forensic investigation.

Yet dollar figures only tell part of the story. Bitcoin’s enormous appreciation over the past decade means an incident that looked comparatively modest when it occurred can dwarf today’s billion-dollar exploits when measured in the quantity of BTC stolen. Meanwhile, the amount initially taken does not necessarily represent the ultimate financial damage, particularly when assets are frozen, recovered, or reimbursed.

The 20 Largest Crypto Hacks Ranked by Dollar Value

The first comparison ranks cryptocurrency thefts by their estimated U.S. dollar values at the time of each incident rather than present-day valuations. It includes exchange breaches, bridge exploits, and unauthorized transfers, although the circumstances of certain cases complicate their classification as conventional hacks. Recoveries and reimbursements are treated separately from the initial amounts compromised.

RankIncidentEstimated Loss
1Binance$6.3B-$6.4B
2Bybit$1.46B-$1.5B
3Ronin Network$540M-$625M
4Poly Network$610M-$613M
5BSC Token Hub$570M-$586M
6Coincheck$530M-$534M
7FTX$450M-$477M
8Mt. Gox$473M
9Bitget$351.6M-$387.5M
10Wormhole$320M-$326M
11Liquid Network$320M
12DMM Bitcoin$305M-$308M
13KelpDAO$292M
14Drift Protocol$285M-$295M
15KuCoin$150M-$280M
16WazirX$230M-$235M
17Cetus Protocol$223M
18Mixin Network$200M
19Euler Finance$197M
20Nomad Bridge$190M

The first striking observation is the distance separating Binance from the rest of the field. Its reported $6.3 billion loss is more than four times the value of Bybit’s February 2025 breach, previously regarded as the industry’s largest single cryptocurrency theft by dollar value.

But even the headline totals demand scrutiny. The BSC Token Hub exploit, for example, involved approximately $570 million in newly minted BNB, although substantially less was successfully moved beyond the affected ecosystem. Similarly, the Poly Network attacker eventually returned most of the stolen assets, illustrating the considerable difference between the initial value compromised and the amount permanently lost.

Binance, Bybit and the Billion-Dollar Era

The Oct. 29 Binance incident represents a new magnitude of reported exchange security failure. Blockchain investigators traced approximately $6.3 billion in transfers across nearly a dozen blockchains, including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, and Solana. Onchain slueths further identified 18,270 BTC among the stolen assets and attributed the operation to North Korea’s Tradertraitor group. Binance, meanwhile, pledged to cover customer balances through its emergency reserves and corporate resources, while partners reportedly froze approximately $3 billion in affected assets.

The Bybit breach on Feb. 21, 2025, previously occupied the top position. Attackers compromised the transaction approval process during an ether cold-wallet transfer, making a malicious transaction appear legitimate to authorized signers. Approximately 400,000 ETH and related assets, valued at around $1.46 billion to $1.5 billion, were stolen. The FBI subsequently attributed the attack to North Korean operatives, while Bybit secured additional liquidity to honor customer withdrawals.

Ronin, Poly Network and the Bridge Exploits

Ronin Network’s March 2022 attack demonstrated how a limited number of compromised validator keys could compromise an entire bridge. Attackers obtained control over five of nine validators and withdrew 173,600 ETH alongside 25.5 million USDC. Depending on the valuation date, the stolen assets were worth approximately $540 million to $625 million. U.S. authorities attributed the operation to North Korea’s Lazarus Group.

Poly Network suffered a different kind of disaster in August 2021. A flaw in the cross-chain protocol’s access controls permitted unauthorized transfers valued at approximately $610 million. Unlike most large cryptocurrency thefts, however, the attacker subsequently returned nearly all the assets, transforming what initially appeared to be a catastrophic loss into one of the industry’s most unusual recovery episodes.

The BSC Token Hub incident in October 2022 involved a vulnerability that permitted the unauthorized creation of 2 million BNB. Although those tokens carried a nominal value approaching $570 million to $586 million, only a fraction escaped the ecosystem before intervention. That distinction matters because newly minted tokens valued at market prices are not necessarily equivalent to immediately realizable proceeds.

Coincheck, FTX and Mt Gox

Japan’s Coincheck lost approximately 523 million NEM tokens in January 2018 after attackers compromised a hot wallet. The assets were worth roughly $530 million at the time, making the incident one of the largest exchange breaches of its era. Coincheck subsequently compensated affected customers using company funds.

FTX experienced an estimated $450 million to $477 million in unauthorized cryptocurrency transfers during its November 2022 collapse. The withdrawals occurred amid bankruptcy proceedings and an extraordinary breakdown in corporate controls. Because the incident coincided with broader insolvency and alleged misuse of customer assets, some historical rankings exclude it from conventional hacking comparisons.

Then there is Mt Gox, whose historical importance is almost impossible to capture using its original dollar valuation. The exchange disclosed approximately 850,000 missing BTC in 2014, including customer and corporate holdings, before locating roughly 200,000 BTC in an old wallet. The initial shortfall was valued around $473 million at bankruptcy, but the remaining loss of approximately 650,000 BTC has become vastly more consequential as bitcoin’s market price has appreciated.

Bitget, Wormhole and Liquid Network

Bitget’s reported September 2026 incident initially carried an estimated value of $351.6 million, subsequently revised to approximately $387.5 million after investigators identified additional affected assets. The supplied research describes compromised withdrawal infrastructure and says the exchange intended to use its protection fund to cover customer losses. Attribution to North Korean actors remains an assessment rather than a confirmed official finding.

Wormhole lost approximately $320 million to $326 million in February 2022 when attackers exploited a signature-validation vulnerability to create 120,000 wrapped ETH without the required backing. Jump Crypto later replenished the missing collateral, preventing the exploit from becoming an equivalent permanent loss for users.

The September 2026 Liquid Network incident involved approximately 4,000 BTC, with the supplied account describing the actors as white-hat hackers who later returned 3,400 BTC. That account requires careful treatment: the claimed return substantially changes the economic impact, and the research does not provide a complete primary-source reconstruction of the event.

DMM Bitcoin, KelpDAO and Drift Protocol

DMM Bitcoin lost 4,502.9 BTC in May 2024, valued at approximately $305 million to $308 million. Investigators tied the theft to North Korean social engineering targeting a wallet-management provider. The Japanese exchange ultimately arranged customer compensation and wound down its operations, showing how a security incident can become an existential business problem even when reimbursement is promised.

Two reported incidents in April 2026 added another estimated $577 million to the industry’s security bill. KelpDAO suffered an approximately $292 million compromise involving off-chain infrastructure, while Drift Protocol lost an estimated $285 million to $295 million. Investigators suspected North Korean involvement in the Drift incident, although the attribution remained provisional in the supplied material.

Kucoin, WazirX, Cetus, Mixin, Euler and Nomad

Kucoin’s September 2020 breach involved compromised hot-wallet private keys and estimates ranging from $150 million to $280 million in affected assets. The exchange subsequently reported recovering a substantial proportion of the funds through tracking, freezes, and cooperation with other platforms, illustrating how coordinated responses can reduce an attack’s lasting financial consequences.

WazirX suffered approximately $230 million to $235 million in losses in July 2024 after a multisignature wallet was compromised. The incident disrupted withdrawals and trading, triggering restructuring and recovery efforts. The attack was attributed to the Lazarus Group, with the custody arrangement itself becoming a central focus of scrutiny.

The remaining cases illustrate how vulnerabilities extend well beyond centralized exchanges. Cetus Protocol’s May 2025 exploit involved approximately $223 million, while Mixin Network reported roughly $200 million in losses in September 2023. Euler Finance lost approximately $197 million in March 2023 through a flash-loan-assisted exploit, although negotiations ultimately resulted in the return of roughly 90% of the stolen funds. Nomad Bridge, meanwhile, suffered an approximately $190 million exploit in August 2022 after a message-validation weakness allowed fraudulent withdrawals.

The Biggest Bitcoin Thefts Tell an Entirely Different Story

Dollar-denominated rankings favor more recent incidents, when cryptocurrency markets commanded substantially higher valuations. Measuring historical thefts by the number of bitcoin stolen produces a dramatically different hierarchy, one dominated by early exchange breaches, compromised wallets, and losses that occurred when BTC traded at a fraction of its present-day price.

For comparison, the ranking table below uses a fixed reference price of $78,000 per bitcoin. These calculations are hypothetical valuations of historical BTC quantities, not estimates of the assets still controlled by attackers or the amounts that could realistically be recovered.

IncidentBTC StolenValue at $78,000
Mt Gox850,000$66.30B
Lubian (disputed)127,426$9.94B
Bitfinex119,756$9.34B
Linode-linked thefts46,653$3.64B
Allinvain wallet25,000$1.95B
Bitstamp18,866$1.47B
Binance (2026)18,270$1.43B
Cryptsy13,000$1.01B
Binance (2019)7,000$546M
DMM Bitcoin4,502.9$351.2M
Liquid Network4,000$312M
Mintpal3,894$303.7M

This comparison changes the entire historical hierarchy. Mt Gox’s original reported shortfall of 850,000 BTC would carry a hypothetical valuation of $66.3 billion at $78,000 per coin, more than ten times the estimated dollar value of the October 2026 Binance incident. Even the approximately 650,000 BTC remaining after the old-wallet discovery would be worth $50.7 billion at the same reference price.

The 2016 Bitfinex theft also becomes considerably more imposing when measured in bitcoin. Attackers took 119,756 BTC, worth approximately $72 million at the time. At the reference price used in this analysis, the same quantity would be worth approximately $9.34 billion, although U.S. authorities subsequently seized a substantial portion of the stolen coins.

Lubian Mining presents another extraordinary but disputed case. Arkham Intelligence alleged that 127,426 BTC was stolen from the mining operation in December 2020 because of weaknesses in private-key generation. The alleged loss would be worth approximately $9.94 billion at $78,000 per coin. However, unresolved questions about ownership, the mechanism, and later U.S. seizure proceedings mean it should not be presented as a conclusively established exchange or mining-pool hack.

Early cryptocurrency history also includes the Linode-linked thefts affecting several businesses in 2012, the reported loss of 25,000 BTC from the wallet known as Allinvain in 2011, and incidents involving Cryptsy, Bitstamp and Mintpal. These cases were financially smaller at contemporary bitcoin prices, but their BTC quantities are enormous compared with many modern exploits.

Binance’s October 2026 incident also warrants inclusion in the bitcoin-denominated comparison, with the exchange recording 18,270 BTC among the assets transferred during the reported outflows. That is separate from the approximately 7,000 BTC stolen from Binance in May 2019. The newer incident’s bitcoin component alone would be worth about $1.43 billion at the $78,000 reference price, although its overall dollar value was driven by a much broader collection of digital assets.

CZ Says the Largest Dollar Theft Is Not the Largest Bitcoin Theft

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, widely known as CZ, addressed the distinction between dollar-denominated losses and bitcoin quantities in a statement supplied for this report. His argument centers on a deceptively simple point: the biggest headline figure does not necessarily identify the most consequential incident for users, markets or the cryptocurrency supply.

“Saw a few discussions about size of hack, why impact to bitcoin price is small, etc. $6.3 billion is the biggest in USD terms, but not in BTC terms. MtGox was 650,000 BTC,” Zhao wrote on X. “Other important numbers to consider: % of bitcoin (in relation to BTC total supply), ie, market impact. MtGox is big there again at 5%+. Number of users impacted, and % of user assets impacted. MtGox (the largest CEX at the time) and FTX (not small) were all near 100% of users and their [assets].”

CZ added:

“Most important: Who is impacted? Does the platform cover it all? (only one victim), as in recent two CEX cases and Binance. Obviously, still a major disaster for the industry, Binance (and me). It hurts, but we survive. Most importantly, we protect our users.”

The statement, reproduced as supplied, raises an important question about how the industry measures security failures. Gross theft figures describe the assets compromised, but they do not reveal how much customers ultimately lose, whether the affected company remains solvent or how much of the stolen cryptocurrency can be recovered.

title: Tether-Backed FASE Foundation Targets Scams and Stablecoin Aid

content:
TL;DR: Named founding stakeholders include Anchorage Digital, Bybit, Chainalysis, Payward, Opera and the Solana Foundation; the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime is a strategic adviser. The education and aid figures are targets, not verified beneficiaries.

On October 28 Tether announced the Swiss not-for-profit Financial Access and Systemic Empowerment Foundation, bringing together businesses and non-profit partners around financial safety, inclusion, access to essential resources and responsible artificial intelligence.

The announcement and the numbers

The most concrete starting point is the dated disclosure from FASE Foundation. It offers a specific basis for assessing Tether-backed FASE Foundation’s anti-scam and aid plans without turning the story into unsupported price speculation.

Named founding stakeholders include Anchorage Digital, Bybit, Chainalysis, Payward, Opera and the Solana Foundation; the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime is a strategic adviser. FASE said an education initiative could reach up to 10 million young people and an aid pilot could potentially serve up to 1 million people.

There is a practical market question underneath the announcement: how quickly can crypto fraud prevention and humanitarian stablecoin pilots change real activity, rather than merely expand a list of proposed services? For investors, the distinction matters because product news and actual changes to liquidity or demand are not interchangeable.

Why the development matters

The question for market participants is what Tether-backed FASE Foundation’s anti-scam and aid plans establishes today and what remains uncertain. An immediate reaction is not the same as evidence of a durable economic outcome.

The initiative is a response to a persistent tension in digital assets: the same global connectivity that makes low-friction payments appealing can also make fraud more scalable. Programs that reach vulnerable populations need outcomes beyond transaction counts.

Custodial exchanges and digital-asset service providers operate several overlapping systems: wallet signing, policy engines, infrastructure permissions, customer ledgers and incident response. A weakness in one layer can matter even when a private key is not publicly exposed. The security story therefore cannot be reduced to a single cryptographic question.

From a market perspective, the first task is to separate the scale of the announcement from the scale of economic activity that has actually occurred. A company may report a large addressable market, an institutional name or a future capability, but those are not equivalent to settled transactions or recurring fee income. This is why the primary disclosure is a better starting point than a trading narrative attached to it.

Risks the headline does not resolve

None of this removes the need for independent assessment. The published evidence identifies a development, while its risk and long-term economics are still open to examination.

Stablecoin aid programs can move a digital claim across borders, but delivering useful support still requires safe wallets, local merchant acceptance, cash-out access, identity protections and appropriate oversight. Anti-scam education likewise depends on accessible language and credible community outreach.

The education and aid figures are targets, not verified beneficiaries. The foundation’s stated ambitions should be distinguished from funded commitments, completed pilots and independent measurements of impact.

Users face two different forms of risk during a security incident. Asset losses are the direct financial concern, while withdrawals, service interruptions and unclear communications can make it difficult to assess or manage exposure. Investigations are strongest when confirmed technical evidence is separated from hypotheses about attackers.

The milestones to watch

The immediate checklist is relatively straightforward: look for verifiable implementation details and avoid interpreting a stated target as an outcome that has already occurred.

The practical follow-up is whether FASE publishes measurable outcomes, safeguards for recipient data and evidence that resources reach people who need them. Its ability to coordinate commercial partners and humanitarian organizations will determine the significance of the announcement.

Investors also need to separate changes in infrastructure from changes in token demand. Revenue may accrue to a company, a protocol treasury or a service provider without necessarily creating a one-for-one benefit for holders of a related token. Market impact depends on adoption, competition and the design of whatever fees or incentives are involved.

A durable signal would be consistent follow-through: actual usage, transparent reporting and a credible explanation of risk. Short-term token-price moves can be driven by macroeconomic conditions or leverage and may say little about whether the product or initiative succeeds over months and years.

title: Binance Hack Jolts Bitcoin Treasury Firm Into Weighing BTC Sales
summary: Next Technology Holding, the 18th-largest publicly traded corporate bitcoin holder at press time, has authorized the sale or pledging of its approximately 5,833 BTC following Binance’s major security incident. The company’s decision reflects mounting concerns about exchange vulnerabilities, internat...
content:
Next Technology Holding, the 18th-largest publicly traded corporate bitcoin holder at press time, has authorized the sale or pledging of its approximately 5,833 BTC following Binance’s major security incident. The company’s decision reflects mounting concerns about exchange vulnerabilities, international cyberattacks, and quantum computing. Although none of its bitcoin is held at Binance, the company is preparing to reduce exposure or tap its holdings for financing.

Key Takeaways

  • Next Technology authorized sales or pledges involving approximately 5,833 bitcoin on Oct. 30.
  • Binance’s security incident prompted Next Technology to reconsider its cryptocurrency exposure.
  • Next Technology cited hacking threats and quantum computing risks, but disclosed no completed bitcoin sales.

Next Technology Holding Eyes Bitcoin Exit as Binance Hack Fuels Security Fears

A company holding 5,833 bitcoin has decided that keeping its digital fortune intact might be a bigger gamble than selling it. Next Technology Holding, one of the world’s largest publicly traded corporate BTC holders, has authorized its executives to sell or pledge the cryptocurrency following Binance’s reported security incident.

The twist? Not a single bitcoin in the company’s treasury was held at Binance. Nevertheless, the security scare, coupled with concerns about artificial intelligence (AI)-driven cyberattacks and the future threat of quantum computing, has prompted a boardroom reassessment of its cryptocurrency exposure.

A Bitcoin Treasury Giant Rethinks Its Position

On Oct. 30, 2026, Next Technology Holding Inc. (Nasdaq: NXTT) announced that its board unanimously approved selling or pledging its bitcoin holdings in one or more tranches. The company, which develops AI-powered software and manages digital assets, held approximately 5,833 BTC as of Oct. 30. Its position ranked 18th among publicly traded corporate bitcoin holders at press time.

The authorization doesn’t mean all 5,833 coins are headed for the exits. Management can sell bitcoin through exchanges, arrange private block trades or pledge the assets as collateral for financing. The board handed its CEO authority over transaction timing, pricing and volume. No completed sale was disclosed in the announcement.

Binance Incident Jolts Corporate Bitcoin Strategy

The board’s decision followed its examination of Binance’s recent security incident, which has raised questions about cryptocurrency custody and exchange defenses. Next Technology emphasized that none of its bitcoin was held through Binance, making its response particularly noteworthy. The company wasn’t reporting a direct loss. Instead, it was reconsidering the risks of owning a substantial cryptocurrency treasury.

The board cited international hacking campaigns, exchange vulnerabilities, and emerging technological threats, including quantum computing, as reasons to reduce exposure and improve liquidity. For a corporate treasury that treats bitcoin as a financial asset, the concern extends beyond whether its own wallets have been compromised. Security failures elsewhere can influence market prices, institutional confidence, and liquidity.

AI Attacks and Quantum Computing Raise the Stakes

The security debate arises as AI-assisted fraud and quantum computing research introduce different challenges for cryptocurrency holders. AI-powered impersonation, deepfake communications and automated social engineering are making attacks against cryptocurrency businesses more sophisticated.

TRM Labs’ reporting found that the use of large language models (LLMs) in scams increased fivefold in 2025. Attackers have increasingly targeted employees, devices and operational controls rather than attempting to defeat blockchain cryptography directly. Quantum computing presents a different problem. No existing quantum computer can break Bitcoin’s signature cryptography, but researchers are investigating how future machines might derive private keys from exposed public keys.

That risk remains prospective, not an active compromise of Bitcoin. Nevertheless, it has entered corporate discussions about the security of long-term digital asset holdings.

Selling Bitcoin or Borrowing Against It?

Next Technology’s announcement leaves considerable room for maneuvering. Pledging bitcoin for financing would allow the company to obtain liquidity without necessarily disposing of its holdings, although collateral arrangements introduce their own financial risks. Outright sales, meanwhile, would reduce its direct exposure to bitcoin price movements.

The company cautioned that there is no guarantee regarding the timing, size or completion of any transaction. “The resolutions approve the sale or pledging of the company’s bitcoin holdings in one or more tranches commencing on the effective date of the consent,” Next Technology’s release explains.

For now, its board has approved the exit doors without requiring management to walk through them. The bigger question is whether other corporate bitcoin holders will interpret security threats as reasons to reconsider their own treasury strategies.

title: Kim Jong Un and North Korea Memes Flood X After Binance’s $6.3B Hack
summary: Crypto Twitter on the social media platform now called X has found its latest villain-turned-comedian in Kim Jong Un. Following the colossal Binance breach, images of the North Korean dictator celebrating an imaginary payday have spread across nearly everyone’s timeline. Beneath the digital mockery ...
content:
Crypto Twitter on the social media platform now called X has found its latest villain-turned-comedian in Kim Jong Un. Following the colossal Binance breach, images of the North Korean dictator celebrating an imaginary payday have spread across nearly everyone’s timeline. Beneath the digital mockery lies a considerably darker financial story involving hundreds of suspected cyberattacks, an expanding network of state-linked hackers, and a staggering accumulation of stolen cryptocurrency.

Key Takeaways

  • Social media’s latest viral punchline carries a far more troubling backstory.
  • A sophisticated operation exploited weaknesses far removed from blockchain cryptography.
  • The difference between stolen wealth and spendable money remains a crucial mystery.

Kim Jong Un Gets the Last Laugh as Crypto’s Biggest Heist Becomes Meme Gold

Apparently, $6.36 billion buys plenty of laughs, particularly when the suspected beneficiaries reside in one of the world’s most heavily sanctioned countries. Following Binance’s Oct. 29 security catastrophe, social media users began depicting Kim Jong Un grinning like a lottery winner, inspecting his imaginary exchange balance and enjoying the finer things in life.

The jokes arrived as blockchain investigators pointed toward North Korea’s notorious Tradertraitor operation, associated with the broader Lazarus Group. But behind the digitally embellished dictator sits a far less amusing reality: a cybercrime enterprise whose suspected cryptocurrency thefts now total approximately $13.3 billion.

Crypto Twitter Gives Pyongyang the Hollywood Treatment

One viral X post imagined Kim celebrating after supposedly increasing his country’s gross domestic product by $6 billion. Another portrayed him congratulating the alleged Binance hacker, with the added punchline that the operative wouldn’t personally receive a cent. The festivities extended to luxury-themed edits, impersonator accounts thanking cryptocurrency investors, and Halloween jokes about a particularly expensive trick-or-treat.

It’s gallows humor with a geopolitical twist. The memes ridicule the apparent failure of sophisticated financial defenses against operatives allegedly working for an isolated authoritarian government. Their popularity also revives an older internet tradition of joking that stolen digital assets finance North Korean missile launches.

A Compromised Laptop Opens a Multibillion-Dollar Door

The alleged attackers reportedly exploited access originating from a Binance engineer’s infected computer, reaching systems authorized to approve withdrawals. Within approximately 20 minutes, assets moved across nearly a dozen blockchains, including 18,270 BTC and substantial quantities of ether, XRP, and stablecoins. Investigators identified advance preparations involving transaction permissions and specialized Ethereum functionality that helped execute the operation.

Binance has pledged to absorb the financial damage, while emergency interventions by token issuers and blockchain administrators reportedly immobilized between $2.7 billion and $3 billion. The company maintained that customer assets were protected. No U.S. government agency had publicly assigned responsibility for the incident as of Oct. 31, leaving the private-sector attribution distinct from an official finding.

Lazarus Group’s Alleged $14B Fortune Has Been Decades in the Making

The broader historical accounting encompasses 296 suspected North Korea-linked cryptocurrency thefts, although individual cases carry different levels of evidentiary support. The progression is striking. A $275 million Kucoin incident in 2020 preceded the $620 million Ronin Bridge exploitation in 2022. DMM Bitcoin lost approximately $308 million in 2024, followed by Bybit’s $1.46 billion catastrophe in February 2025.

Federal authorities attributed the Ronin, DMM Bitcoin, and Bybit incidents to North Korean actors. Other cases remain supported primarily by blockchain intelligence assessments rather than government findings. The organization itself is no ordinary hacking outfit. Lazarus functions as an umbrella designation encompassing overlapping North Korean cyber operations, including financially motivated units such as Bluenoroff and Tradertraitor.

The Billion-Dollar Question Nobody Can Answer With a Meme

The techniques have changed considerably since the hacking syndicate‘s earlier banking exploits. Fake recruitment offers, malicious software, compromised transaction interfaces and deceptive authorization requests now feature prominently in investigations. After an intrusion, stolen assets can pass through intermediary wallets, token swaps and laundering services designed to complicate tracing and recovery.

Crucially, historical theft valuations do not establish how much money reached the North Korean government. They include assets later recovered, immobilized or rendered inaccessible, alongside incidents whose attribution remains disputed. That leaves the internet’s favorite image of a laughing dictator with one rather expensive missing detail: whether Pyongyang can actually spend the fortune everyone keeps joking about.

title: Shopify’s Base USDC Checkout Puts Stablecoins Into Mainstream E-Commerce

title: Bitcoin ETFs Lose $643M After Binance Hack Ends 4-Day Inflow Run
summary: Bitcoin ETFs suffered $643.33 million in net outflows Friday, wiping out four consecutive days of inflows and pushing the week into negative territory. Ether and solana also faced heavy redemptions as the Binance hack triggered a fresh bout of risk aversion across crypto markets. Blackrock, Fidelity...
content:
Bitcoin ETFs suffered $643.33 million in net outflows Friday, wiping out four consecutive days of inflows and pushing the week into negative territory. Ether and solana also faced heavy redemptions as the Binance hack triggered a fresh bout of risk aversion across crypto markets.

Key Takeaways

  • Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) lost $643.33M on Friday, erasing four days of inflows and turning the week negative.
  • Ether lost $155.85M, and solana lost $10.74M as the Binance breach deepened crypto risk aversion.
  • Friday’s high-volume selloff shows security shocks can rapidly overwhelm institutional accumulation.

Blackrock, Fidelity Lead $643M Bitcoin ETF Selloff

Four days of steady accumulation disappeared in a single session.

Bitcoin ETFs had gathered $440.73 million from Monday through Thursday. Friday’s $643.33 million withdrawal erased that cushion and left the week roughly $202.6 million in the red.

The selling was broad. Blackrock’s IBIT lost $233.70 million, Fidelity’s FBTC shed $201.04 million, and Ark & 21Shares’ ARKB recorded a $129.55 million exit. Grayscale’s GBTC lost another $53.32 million, while Bitwise’s BITB shed $25.72 million.

Trading value surged to $6.35 billion, roughly three times Thursday’s level. Net assets fell below $100 billion to $98.14 billion.

A Broader Retreat Than Earlier October Reversals

The breadth of Friday’s selling carries more weight than the headline total.

Earlier in the week, Bitcoin ETF inflows were often concentrated in IBIT. Friday brought redemptions across five major products at once. That suggests the risk reduction reached beyond a single portfolio or fund complex.

Bitcoin’s price also faced a much less forgiving backdrop after news of the Binance security breach spread through the market. The hack unfolded after Thursday’s U.S. ETF session, making Friday the first full trading day in which ETF investors could react. Still, ETF data show where money moved, not why individual investors sold.

Ether’s Difficult Week Gets Worse

Ether ETFs lost $155.85 million on Friday, their fifth consecutive daily outflow.

Blackrock’s ETHA shed $76.64 million. Its ETHB product lost $19.51 million, while Grayscale’s Ether Mini Trust and ETHE posted withdrawals of $34.14 million and $21.51 million.

Fidelity’s FETH and Morgan Stanley’s MSSE also finished negative.

That pushed ether’s weekly outflow to roughly $431.5 million, extending a pattern of sustained institutional selling that has now lasted well beyond isolated weak sessions.

Solana ETFs lost another $10.74 million, taking weekly withdrawals to about $71.5 million.

Security Risk Moves Back to the Foreground

Zcash finally broke its eight-session inflow streak, losing $4.57 million through Grayscale’s ZCSH. XRP saw a modest $496,500 exit, while HYPE and NEAR recorded no net flows.

The Binance breach also revived questions about custody concentration across institutional crypto products.

OneKey founder Yishi Wang warned that large bitcoin vehicles such as Blackrock’s IBIT could become attractive targets for sophisticated attackers. His comments described a hypothetical security risk, and there is no evidence that IBIT itself has been targeted.

Friday’s flows leave a striking end to the week.

Bitcoin began with four straight inflow sessions. Ether selling never stopped. Solana remained under pressure. Then one high-volume session overwhelmed nearly every positive trend that had developed since Monday.

For crypto ETFs, security risk has suddenly returned to the center of the allocation debate.

title: XTB CEO Says Broker Was “a Bit Late” to the UK as Indonesia Trails Only Poland
summary:
XTB's chief executive said on Thursday that the Polish broker had probably arrived in the UK late. Omar Arnaout told a third-quarter results conference that competing there with established local firms would take very large sums, and that he would approach the market very cautiously.
In the same ans...
content:
2026-10-31T21:56:30.914+02:00

Saturday, 31/10/2026 | 19:56 GMT by Damian Chmiel

  • Omar Arnaout said competing with established British firms would take far bigger marketing budgets.
  • Its Asian unit added commodity CFDs in August, with a read on demand due within five weeks.

XTB's chief executive said on Thursday that the Polish broker had probably arrived in the UK late. Omar Arnaout told a third-quarter results conference that competing there with established local firms would take very large sums, and that he would approach the market very cautiously.

In the same answer, he said Indonesia now signs up more accounts each month than any XTB market except Poland. The conference followed a fourfold rise in XTB's third-quarter profit to PLN 213.7 million (about $54.4 million), reported on Wednesday.

Both countries were set up as tests for 2026. In January, Arnaout said this would be a test year for the UK, and in March he told FinanceMagnates.com that Indonesia, then a country with a question mark, had six months to prove itself.

London's trading industry is coming home!

A Late Start in Britain

The UK business is small next to the platforms it competes with. XTB's British unit more than doubled its revenue to £8.64 million (about $11.6 million) in 2025, while Trading 212 booked £277.6 million in the UK over the same year.

That puts XTB's British revenue at about 3% of its rival's, by FinanceMagnates.com's calculation.

"I think we were simply a bit late to this market," Arnaout said.

XTB launched a zero-fee stocks and shares ISA in December 2024 and added a cash ISA this year. It ran 11,767 ISA and cash ISA accounts at the end of September, up from 10,717 three months earlier, according to its quarterly reports.

The gain of about 1,050 accounts compares with the 152,000 customers AJ Bell added in the 12 months to September, as British platforms and CFD brokers compete for the same tax-free savers.

Where the Marketing Money Goes

title: CFTC and US Lawmaker Offer Two Different Answers to Binance’s $6.3B Hack
summary: A $6.3 billion crypto heist has handed Washington a fresh regulatory fight. One federal watchdog wants exchanges to volunteer for oversight, while a Republican senator argues Congress already missed its chance to give the industry stronger defenses against thieves. CFTC Chair Selig Pushes Federal Re...
content:
A $6.3 billion crypto heist has handed Washington a fresh regulatory fight. One federal watchdog wants exchanges to volunteer for oversight, while a Republican senator argues Congress already missed its chance to give the industry stronger defenses against thieves.

Key Takeaways

  • CFTC Chairman Michael Selig proposes voluntary federal oversight following Binance’s $6.3 billion hack.
  • Sen. Cynthia Lummis argues the stalled CLARITY Act would have strengthened emergency freeze protections.
  • Binance reportedly froze $3 billion as Washington debates how to prevent another massive theft.

CFTC Chair Selig Pushes Federal Registration After Binance Theft

The Oct. 29 Binance breach, reportedly involving around $6.3 billion in stolen cryptocurrency, has become an unlikely catalyst for two competing regulatory arguments. Both promise better protection, but they take distinctly different routes through Washington.

Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chairman Michael Selig used an Oct. 30 CNBC interview to advocate voluntary federal registration for cryptocurrency exchanges, including offshore platforms such as Binance. Selig emphasized:

“We want to offer these exchanges a federal option to come and register with the CFTC.”

His proposal would let eligible exchanges enter a federal supervisory framework covering cybersecurity, market manipulation, customer protections, and custody safeguards. The catch? Washington cannot compel every centralized cryptocurrency exchange (CEX) to register without additional congressional authority.

Selig’s approach builds on an Oct. 5 regulatory initiative proposing Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM, which would establish tailored oversight for certain leveraged, margined or financed retail cryptocurrency transactions.

Lummis Blames Stalled CLARITY Act for Lost Protection

Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., sees another problem: Congress failed to advance legislation she believes would have helped authorities respond faster.

“Every minute lost is money gone for good,” Lummis wrote on X on Oct. 30, arguing the stalled CLARITY Act would have provided legal protections for firms freezing suspicious transactions at law enforcement’s request.

The legislation failed a Senate procedural vote on Sept. 15, falling short of the 60 votes needed to advance. Lummis subsequently drew fire from Amanda Fischer of Better Markets, who disputed her interpretation. Fischer argued that existing mechanisms already permitted voluntary freezes and that the proposed legislation would not have changed those actions.

Lummis countered on social media, saying that the bill’s provisions concerning covered digital asset service providers would have offered additional authority and reduced liability risks. “No law stops every bad actor, but the Clarity Act would have given the people fighting them better tools and the ability to act faster. Your party voted no, and you have to own that. Thanks for playing, Amanda Fischer,” Lummis wrote.

Billions Frozen as Washington Debates Its Next Move

The argument isn’t entirely academic. Binance reportedly coordinated with partners to freeze approximately $3 billion following the theft, nearly half the estimated losses, while promising to cover affected customer balances. Meanwhile, Selig’s regulatory proposal remains preliminary, with public comments open until Dec. 14. Neither a voluntary registration pathway nor the stalled legislation offers an immediate remedy for the stolen assets.

One proposal asks exchanges to accept federal supervision. The other seeks stronger statutory authority to intervene when criminals strike. The uncomfortable question is whether either would have stopped the Binance attackers before billions disappeared.

title: Chainlink Unveils 24/7 Pricing for Tokenized Assets as Aave Adopts Feeds
summary: The service extends a prior 24/5 equity-data product into weekends and holidays. An oracle feed is not a guarantee of a redeemable cash-market price,
content:
TL;DR: The service extends a prior 24/5 equity-data product into weekends and holidays. An oracle feed is not a guarantee of a redeemable cash-market price, and an off-hours derivative reference can diverge from the next opening auction.

Chainlink introduced its 24/7 data service on October 29 to supply reference prices for equities, commodities and other real-world assets beyond conventional exchange hours. It identified lending protocol Aave as the launch partner for using the feeds to value eligible collateral.

The announcement and the numbers

The most concrete starting point is the dated disclosure from Chainlink. It offers a specific basis for assessing Chainlink’s round-the-clock real-world asset price feeds without turning the story into unsupported price speculation.

The service extends a prior 24/5 equity-data product into weekends and holidays. Chainlink said off-hours references combine information from several perpetual-futures venues, with stale data filtering and outlier controls, rather than treating a closed stock exchange as if it were still publishing live prices.

Announcements in crypto often arrive before the data needed to price their longer-term significance. A sensible reading separates what has already been delivered from what still needs commercial adoption, technical validation or regulatory clearance.

Why the development matters

The question for market participants is what Chainlink’s round-the-clock real-world asset price feeds establishes today and what remains uncertain. An immediate reaction is not the same as evidence of a durable economic outcome.

Continuous reference data can support longer trading sessions, lending and prediction markets. The larger question is whether financial risk engines can make defensible decisions on Saturday using prices derived from instruments whose liquidity and economics differ from the underlying asset.

A pilot, framework or technical partnership should not be conflated with a live secondary market. Investors need to know whether assets have actually been issued, whether redemption is possible and where responsibility sits if records disagree.

A durable signal would be consistent follow-through: actual usage, transparent reporting and a credible explanation of risk. Short-term token-price moves can be driven by macroeconomic conditions or leverage and may say little about whether the product or initiative succeeds over months and years.

Risks the headline does not resolve

None of this removes the need for independent assessment. The published evidence identifies a development, while its risk and long-term economics are still open to examination.

A tokenized share can trade or support a loan when the underlying cash market is closed, creating a mismatch between token liquidity and reference pricing. Oracles deliver data to smart contracts, but the usefulness of a quote depends on its source quality, freshness and suitability for liquidation decisions.

An oracle feed is not a guarantee of a redeemable cash-market price, and an off-hours derivative reference can diverge from the next opening auction. Protocols need conservative collateral factors, circuit breakers and governance around unusual market conditions.

Representing an asset on a blockchain is the relatively straightforward part of tokenization. Making that representation useful requires legal rights, reliable valuation, restrictions on eligible holders, custody and a clear process for settlement and corporate actions.

The milestones to watch

The immediate checklist is relatively straightforward: look for verifiable implementation details and avoid interpreting a stated target as an outcome that has already occurred.

Watch which assets gain coverage, how Aave manages liquidations outside exchange hours, and whether data stays robust during thin liquidity. Sustainable usage is more important than a claim that a particular market is now technically available every hour.

From a market perspective, the first task is to separate the scale of the announcement from the scale of economic activity that has actually occurred. A company may report a large addressable market, an institutional name or a future capability, but those are not equivalent to settled transactions or recurring fee income. This is why the primary disclosure is a better starting point than a trading narrative attached to it.

Investors also need to separate changes in infrastructure from changes in token demand. Revenue may accrue to a company, a protocol treasury or a service provider without necessarily creating a one-for-one benefit for holders of a related token. Market impact depends on adoption, competition and the design of whatever fees or incentives are involved.

Primary source: Chainlink’s primary announcement. This reporting reflects information available on October 31, 2026; targets, estimates and statements about future plans are attributed to their issuers.

This article was written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.
